newsitem.title: UK: UK government eyes 10-15 pct level for water leaks.
newsitem.headline: UK government eyes 10-15 pct level for water leaks.

text.p: The amount of water currently leaking out of pipelines in Britain is "appalling," and the government would like to see it reduced to levels around 10-15 percent of supplies, environment minister Michael Meacher told a press conference on Tuesday.

"There's no question of an economic leakage level being anything like as high as 26 percent," Meacher said, adding that New York has around 10-15 percent of supplies seeping out of its system. "That's the kind of thing we're looking for."
The new centre-left Labour government has made mandatory targets for cutting leaks a key part of a 10-point plan launched at a crisis summit for the industry in May.
The targets will be set in conjunction with industry regulator Ofwat.
Companies have been responding "positively" to the plan, according to deputy prime minister John Prescott, and all are now offering free leak repair services to customers on their main pipes.
Britain's water companies have come under heavy criticism for high shareholder payouts and executive pay packets.

They came under further fire during Britain's driest period for 200 years over 1995 and 1996 as curbs were imposed on some domestic use of water while nearly 800 million gallons of water seeped out of pipes daily.
Labour has also targeted the companies for a 1.65 billion stg share of a 5.2 billion levy on the excess profits of utilities, privatised under previous Conservative governments.

Prescott said he would be writing to companies again by the end of the year to track their progress in complying with targets set out in the 10-point plan, adding that powers could be used through the regulator to bring any laggards into line.
He suggested that high dividend payouts and profits should not come at the expense of fulfilling the targets of the 10-point plan.
"No doubt if (the regulator) thinks they've been making excess profits he might want to take it away (at the next price review, due in 1999)," he added.
